items.title: Black Friday OLED TV deals start at $699, with up to $1,400 off LG, Sony & Samsung
items.content_html:
Black Friday OLED TV deals have dropped LG's 55-inch B6E to $699.99 at Best Buy, with savings reaching up to $1,400 off larger, premium models from LG, Sony, and Samsung.

OLED televisions use self-lit pixels to deliver deep blacks, rich colors, and precise contrast without the backlighting found in conventional LED TVs. Their higher prices have traditionally been a barrier, but the latest discounts put several 2026 models within reach of shoppers looking to upgrade.

Get OLED Black Friday deals

Best Buy has discounted LG's B6E, C6, and G6 lineups, along with competing models from Sony and Samsung. Amazon is also matching Best Buy's $1,399.99 price on the 65-inch LG C6.

Black Friday OLED TV deals start at $699.99

Here are six OLED TV deals worth considering:

  • LG 55-inch B6E OLED - $699.99 ($700 off) at Best Buy
  • LG 65-inch B6E OLED - $999.99 ($900 off) at Best Buy
  • Sony 65-inch BRAVIA 6 OLED - $1,199.99 ($800 off) at Best Buy
  • LG 65-inch C6 OLED - $1,399.99 ($1,300 off) at Amazon and Best Buy
  • Samsung 65-inch S90H OLED - $1,399.99 ($1,300 off) at Amazon and Best Buy
  • LG 65-inch G6 OLED - $1,999.99 ($1,400 off) at Best Buy

LG's B6E offers the least expensive way into the lineup, with Dolby Vision, a 120Hz refresh rate, and support for NVIDIA G-Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium. Its Alpha 8 AI Processor Gen3 handles picture processing, while LG's webOS platform provides access to streaming apps.

The 65-inch B6E is particularly appealing at $999.99, giving buyers 10 more inches of screen size (measured diagonally) for $300 more. Both sizes share the same core features, making the decision largely a matter of budget and available space.

For another $200, Sony's 65-inch BRAVIA 6 brings the company's picture processing and Google TV platform into the mix. It supports Dolby Vision and 4K gaming at 120Hz, making it another option for movies, streaming, and console gaming.

LG's C6 and Samsung's S90H compete directly at $1,399.99, although they take different approaches. The C6 uses Brightness Booster technology and LG's Alpha 11 AI Processor Gen3, while Samsung emphasizes its Glare Free screen treatment to reduce distracting reflections.

Both support refresh rates up to 165Hz with compatible gaming PCs, giving them an advantage over the 120Hz models for high-refresh-rate gaming. However, LG supports Dolby Vision, while Samsung uses HDR10+ instead.

LG OLED AI television

At the top of the list, LG's 65-inch G6 costs $1,999.99 after a $1,400 discount. Its higher brightness, Reflection Free Premium technology, and gallery-style design make it appealing for wall-mounted installations, although buyers should know that the included flush wall mount doesn't come with a tabletop stand.

All six televisions can connect to an Apple TV 4K through HDMI, and AirPlay support lets iPhone, iPad, and Mac users stream compatible content directly to the televisions. Apple TV 4K owners who want Dolby Vision should consider the LG or Sony models, since Samsung doesn't support the format.

For most shoppers, the 65-inch LG B6E at $999.99 offers the strongest combination of screen size, features, and price. The C6 and S90H provide worthwhile upgrades for buyers who prioritize gaming or reflection handling, while the G6 caters to those willing to pay more for premium picture performance and design.

Prices and availability may change throughout the Black Friday shopping period.

items.title: Black Friday streaming deals cut Apple TV to $6.99/mo, Paramount Plus to $2.99/mo
items.content_html:
Black Friday deals are cutting streaming costs by more than 50%, with Apple TV, Paramount+, and other popular services offering steep discounts for new and eligible returning subscribers.

The discounts are already live ahead of Black Friday on November 27, giving subscribers a chance to save on several popular streaming services. Some promotions last six months, while others offer steep discounts on shorter subscriptions.

Apple TV and Crunchyroll are among the services offering longer promotional periods. Paramount+ has one of the biggest monthly discounts, and Amazon is cutting prices on several Prime Video add-ons by as much as 75%.

Get Black Friday streaming deals

Apple TV drops to $6.99 per month for Black Friday

Apple TV is offering six months of streaming for $6.99 per month through Apple TV direct or via Prime Video, down from its regular $14.99 subscription price.

The Black Friday deal saves subscribers $8 per month, or $48 over the full promotional period. New and qualified returning subscribers can claim the discount through November 30.

Get Apple TV BF deal

Apple TV includes original series such as Severance, Slow Horses, Foundation, and Ted Lasso, along with Apple's growing collection of original films.

Sports fans also get Formula 1, Major League Soccer, and Friday Night Baseball as part of the subscription, without an additional sports package.

The six-month discount makes Apple TV one of the better options for anyone planning to keep a streaming service beyond the holidays. Subscribers will return to the regular $14.99 monthly rate after the promotional period unless they cancel.

Paramount+, Crunchyroll, and Starz offer bigger discounts

Paramount+ is cutting both its Essential and Premium plans to $2.99 per month for the first two months, with the offer available through November 30.

Premium normally costs $13.99 per month, making the discounted subscription nearly 80% cheaper. Subscribers will pay $5.98 for two months instead of $27.98, saving $22.

The Premium plan includes Showtime programming, offline downloads, and mostly ad-free on-demand streaming. Paramount+ Essential normally costs $8.99 per month, but its promotional price is identical to Premium's.

New subscribers and eligible former customers can claim the offer, although returning customers may need to sign up through certain supported platforms.

Crunchyroll is running a longer Black Friday promotion for anime fans, dropping its Fan membership from $9.99 to $3.99 per month for six months.

Paramount+ is cutting both its Essential and Premium plans

The Crunchyroll deal saves $36 over six months and includes ad-free access to the service's anime library.

Mega Fan is also discounted to $5.99 per month, down from $13.99. Subscribers who want the additional benefits can save $48 over the same six-month period.

Starz has an even bigger bargain for anyone willing to pay upfront. Its annual subscription costs $11.99 for the entire first year, down from the regular $69.99 annual price.

The annual offer works out to about $1 per month and saves $58 compared with the usual yearly subscription.

Starz also has a monthly promotion at $2.99 per month for three months, down from $11.99. Both offers are available to new subscribers and eligible former customers signing up directly through Starz.

The annual plan is particularly attractive compared with Amazon's Starz promotion, which provides just two months at $2.99 per month. However, Starz automatically changes its annual promotional subscription to monthly billing at the then-current rate after the first year unless canceled.

Prime Video Black Friday deals start at $1.75 per month

Amazon is also offering Black Friday discounts on several Prime Video channels, with subscriptions starting at less than $2 per month.

Get Prime Video BF deals

The promotions are available through Prime Video's add-on subscriptions, letting customers manage multiple streaming services through one account.

Some of the best deals include:

  • MGM+: $1.99 per month for two months, down from $7.99. Get deal.
  • AMC+ Premium: $2.75 per month for two months, down from $10.99. Get deal.
  • BritBox: $2.75 per month for two months, down from $10.99. Get deal.
  • PBS Masterpiece: $1.75 per month for two months, down from $6.99. Get deal.
  • Hallmark+: $2.25 per month for three months, down from $8.99. Get deal.

Hallmark+ stands out for holiday viewing, with three months of discounted streaming instead of the two offered by most participating channels. Its catalog includes Christmas movies and original programming, making the promotion particularly well-timed.

BritBox and PBS Masterpiece offer inexpensive ways to catch up on British dramas and mysteries, while MGM+ and AMC+ provide additional movies and original series.

Prime Video Black Friday deals start at $1.75 per month

Amazon also carries discounted subscriptions to Apple TV, Paramount+, and Crunchyroll, so existing Prime Video customers can get many of the same deals without signing up directly through each service.

A Prime membership or standalone Prime Video subscription is required to purchase these add-on channels. The discounted prices don't include the cost of that underlying subscription.

Black Friday streaming deals won't last forever

Most of these Black Friday streaming discounts are scheduled to end November 30, which is Cyber Monday. However, the length of the promotional subscription matters just as much as the advertised price.

Apple TV and Crunchyroll offer six months of savings, while Paramount+ and most Prime Video channels provide only two discounted months. Starz offers the strongest long-term bargain for customers willing to pay $11.99 upfront for a year.

The promotions generally renew automatically at their regular prices when the discounted periods end, and eligibility varies between services.

Anyone planning to subscribe should check the renewal price before completing checkout. These Black Friday deals can make streaming considerably cheaper, but keeping several subscriptions after their promotions expire can quickly erase those savings.

items.title: Apple supplier TSMC cuts off China chip orders amid tighter export controls
items.content_html:
TSMC, a key Apple supplier and the company that makes its A- and M-series iPhone and Mac chips, has suspended some advanced chip orders for Chinese companies following the tightening of United States semiconductor export restrictions.

Under the revised rules, TSMC can no longer provide Chinese companies with chips built using the 16nm or smaller manufacturing process. That is, unless a U.S. export license has been granted or they qualify for an exemption.

This new restriction means that Chinese companies are limited to chips that use much older technology built on the 28nm or 40nm processes. As a result, they will not be able to make use of the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) employed by AI data centers.

That may be key to the tightening restrictions. U.S. company Nvidia, which is going through its own struggles, is at the forefront of the AI chip market. By limiting Chinese companies to older chip technology, the U.S. could hope to protect Nvidia from growing competition.

A change in process

Impact Newswire reports that, prior to this recent change, TSMC was able to assess a customer's chip designs and then determine whether they qualified for an exemption to U.S. export requirements. But that's now changed, with Chinese companies needing to get a license or exemption ahead of time.

That has left TSMC in a difficult position, and it's told customers that they must suspend orders of 16nm chips or smaller. The orders will resume if customers secure U.S. approval.

While the U.S. does maintain a list of approved companies, none of them are Chinese companies. The list includes the likes of Apple, AMD, and Nvidia.

TSMC has said that it intends to comply with the new law changes around export controls to Chinese companies. That's unsurprising given the possible fallout if it chose not to.

TSMC relies heavily on custom from U.S. companies like Apple, and not complying with export rules could put that business in jeopardy. Aside from the potential fines associated with non-compliance, U.S. companies could be barred from doing business with TSMC entirely.

The company also uses U.S. electronic design automation (EDA) software to manufacture its most advanced chips. Losing access to that software could be catastrophic for TSMC's business.

items.title: First iPhone Air 2 & iPhone 18 dummy units don't have any surprises
items.content_html:
With Apple expected to announce the iPhone Air 2 and iPhone 18 in early 2027, the first dummy units have been photographed and appear to confirm that the iPhone Air's biggest problem will finally be addressed.

September 2026 saw Apple change the way it announces iPhones, with just the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo unveiled. But early 2027 is set to see Apple announce yet more models as it switches to a twice-yearly release cadence.

As part of that, the iPhone Air 2 and iPhone 18 are expected to be joined by the iPhone 18e in the spring of 2027. Now, two of those devices appear to have debuted in dummy unit form.

Shared by serial leaker Sonny Dickson via his X social media account, two images show the front and back of the devices. There are few surprises for those who have been following along with recent rumors, but confirmation of what we can expect is always welcome.

The big changes

The most notable change that iPhone Air 2 buyers can look forward to is the addition of a second camera. The current iPhone Air has a single 48-megapixel camera, and that's something that has long been a knock against that device for some.

With iPhone Air 2, Apple is expected to add a second camera in the form of an ultra wide option. There won't be any optical zoom here, though, so you'll still need an iPhone 18 Pro model for that.

One change that isn't shown in the dummy unit for obvious reasons is the chip. The iPhone Air 2 is set to use the A20 Pro, bringing improved performance and battery life.

We've also been told to expect the iPhone Air 2 to be even thinner than its predecessor, too. But Dickson didn't share measurements, and it's hard to tell from the photos.

As for the base-model iPhone 18, that's set to use the A20 chip and be the cut-down Pro model that we're accustomed to. We don't expect there to be any major design changes compared with the previous-gen iPhone 17, although new colors are likely.

items.title: 24-inch M6 iMac review: Aggressively fine
items.content_html:
The new iMac keeps a great but stale design, and adds a real AI boost with the M6 processor. From $1,499, it is charming, albeit profoundly iterative.

Some products barely need changing, and the iMac is one of them. Apple knows it. The M6 iMac looks exactly like the model before it, because the changes are once again all on the inside.

This year, the trend since the last model released has been the expansion of artificial intelligence tools. Apple is aware of that too, so the M6 chip brings a much faster Neural Engine for on-device AI.

Keep the much-loved shell for a few years, semi-quietly upgrade the parts, and repeat. The same as it has ever been for iMac.

iMac M6 review: Design

Nothing has changed on the outside. That isn't really a giant criticism, because the iMac remains one of Apple's most attractive and identifiable machines.

iMac M6 review: The colors are still more vibrant on the back of the iMac

It remains a housing for the 4.5K Retina display inside a slim aluminum chassis, with the whole computer hiding behind the screen on a simple stand.

The seven colors are back, from blue and green to a bright orange. This is still a machine designed to be seen on a desk, not tucked away under it.

iMac M6 review: The green HomePod mini 2 matches perfectly with the iMac

That look also explains who buys it, with people who care about styling or pops of color the prime target. The iMac suits a family kitchen, a home office, or a creative's tidy desk.

It is also for people who want one clean object, not a tower trailing cables. For them, the all-in-one form is the entire appeal.

The familiar limits do remain, though. The stand still does not adjust for height or tilting, unlike many cheap arms you can find on Amazon.

Hiding every port around the back helps keep things clean, but it's still an annoyance to reach around like any other desktop with rear ports, ever.

iMac M6 review: The power supply connected to the M6 iMac on the back

There is also still only one size. If you want a screen larger than 24 inches, the iMac cannot help you. And, it may never again unless you add a big external display.

iMac M6 review: Small, but mighty updates

The M6 chip is the heart of this update. It arrives in two tiers, and the gap between them matters.

The entry model pairs a 10-core CPU with a 10-core GPU, while the step-up version moves both to 12 cores.

iMac M6 review: The new iMac may be look the same, but it's much faster

Both gain Apple's new dual 16-core Neural Engine, which is the part driving most of the big on-device AI claims. It's not the entire story, since those GPU cores also have Neural Accelerators to handle AI workloads.

Memory starts at a healthier 16 gigabytes this time around. It tops out at 24GB on the base chip, or 32GB on the faster one.

iMac M6 review: Power button on the back-left of the iMac

That 32GB ceiling still feels modest for a 2026 desktop. It sits a little awkwardly beside all the AI ambition and chatter about it in Apple marketing materials.

iMac M6 review: The new WI-Fi 7 is a welcomed addition

That said, anyone who is seriously into AI will be looking at a Mac Studio or beefy Mac mini, not the iMac.

Connectivity moves forward in sensible steps. With the 2026 version, you get Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and up to four Thunderbolt 4 ports.

Note that this is Thunderbolt 4, not the Thunderbolt 5 of the pricier Macs. The latter is for premium Mac models, not for the more consumer-oriented hardware like this.

Thunderbolt 5 will eventually come to the iMac. Just not this year.

iMac M6 review: The ports are located on the back of the iMac

The lower-tier $1,499 model has just two ports and drives a single external display, as well as the 10-core chip. The $1,699 model adds two more ports and support for two external displays in total, as well as higher performance.

The upper model also has Touch ID as standard and the option of nano-texture glass. The faster model includes 2.5-gigabit Ethernet as well, while the base model can add it for just $30.

iMac M6 review: Performance

Apple frames the M6 almost entirely against the M4. The company claims up to twice the graphics performance in photo editing. On-device AI is pitched at up to five times faster.

Everyday apps like Excel are said to be around 1.5 times quicker. The SSD is rated at up to twice the read and write speed.

iMac M6 review: The dock and chin of the iMac

The actual speed delivered varies greatly based on workload. It's hard to see a scenario where a user says "wow, Excel is so much faster on the M6 iMac instead of the M4." Users just don't upgrade iMacs that rapidly.

The iMac remains fast, with far more power than most people need for web, photos, and office work. Local image tools and language models are where the M6 should visibly pull ahead.

When it comes to benchmarks, Geekbench 7 provides a clear sign that things have moved on since M4.

iMac M6 review: Geekbench 7 single-core results

For single-core performance, the M6 models score about 3,900. The M4 generation managed in the ballpark of 3,000, which is a fair bit behind the new ones.

iMac M6 review: Geekbench 7 multi-core results

Multi-core provides a similar evolutionary leap in both variants. The M6 10-core model's 18,000 score is well above the 10-core of the M4 version's 15,000, with the 12-core M6 improving further to over 20,000.

iMac M6 review: Geekbench 7 Metal results

It's a very similar story for Metal, but at a more seismic level. At 81,000 and 87,000, the M6 models are close to double the Metal performance over their predecessors.

The M4 is still great. There's just a lot more headroom when it comes to the M6 models.

iMac M6 review: Still a bargain

The iMac remains one of the easiest Macs to recommend. It is complete, colorful, and starts at a fair $1,499.

You are buying a whole computer, a fine 4.5K display included. Against a separate Mac mini and monitor, the math still holds up.

iMac M6 review: You can optionally get a 2.5Gb Ethernet port on the power adapter

When it comes to upgrades, there's little reason for M4 iMac owners to rush to this model. There's a performance boost, but there are better options for those who really want to dig into AI workflows.

Coming from an Intel or M1 machine, though, this is a huge leap. It's been enough time that M1 upgraders will feel that the improvements are worth it.

iMac M6 review: Apple's latest iMac with the HomeView and green HomePod mini 2

If you're in the market for the new iMac, just buy the 12-core model if you can stretch to it. The extra $200 quietly fixes most of the base model's compromises.

iMac M6 review: Pros

  • Gorgeous 24-inch 4.5K design in seven colors
  • Big on-device AI gains from the M6
  • Still strong value, starting at $1,499

iMac M6 review: Cons

  • Base 10-core model is notably cut down
  • Memory still caps at 32GB
  • Thunderbolt 4, and the same non-adjustable stand

iMac M6 rating: 4 out of 5

This is another case where the hardware is excellent, but not revolutionary. The speed boost is nice, the Wi-Fi improvements will matter more in a few years than they do now, and so forth.

The iMac is still a home and education machine, for the most part. Like I've said before, schools like their portables, but the iMac is still a frequent purchase as they have a tendency to disappear less, and stay pristine longer.

The days of the $499 Microcenter sale on iMacs are long past. The two price increases on the iMac in less than six months are extremely unfortunate.

If you're in the market for an iMac, you're in it for the screen. About 90% of what you're going to do on an iMac, if screen size doesn't matter, will be done at about the same speed on a MacBook Air or MacBook Neo, so think about those even if portability is not your main concern.

And the difference in price between a M6 Mac mini with a keyboard, mouse, and nice external monitor is negligible, so that's a thought too.

Ultimately, the M6 iMac is not a reinvention, and it does not try to be one either. It's good, but also uninspiring. And, it sits in a complex and densely-settled place on Apple's pricing ladder.

And that's all okay.

Where to buy Apple's M6 iMac

Apple's M6 iMac starts at $1,499, with Apple resellers Amazon, B&H, Adorama, and Expercom all selling the all-in-one-desktop.

Expercom, in particular, is already discounting the M6 models by as much as $180.

You can shop the latest deals across the retail and CTO models in our M6 iMac Price Guide.

items.title: No World Cup for Apple as bidding exceeds $1.5 billion
items.content_html:
Apple TV has followed Disney and Skydance in reportedly backing out of bidding for the rights to screen the 2030 and 2034 FIFA World Cup.

Apple promoted the 2026 World Cup by adding comprehensive coverage to its Apple Sports app. It was seen as the company's move toward gaining a larger international audience for sport, but Apple will not now bid to screen the soccer matches.

According to Sports Media Watch, Apple is the latest to withdraw from the bidding. It's not clear at what stage Apple withdrew, but it appears to have elected not to enter the bidding at all.

The reason is presumed to be the price that the tournament is expected to fetch. It's estimated that World Cup rights would cost more than $1.5 billion.

So far Apple's biggest single investment in sport has been a reported $250 million/year for its Major League Soccer coverage. Even that is ending years earlier than planned, suggesting that it didn't boost Apple TV viewership as much as hoped.

Skydance has just spent $110 billion acquiring Warner Bros. Discovery, so it is said to be planning cost-cutting. The price tag is also the reason that Disney will not be bidding.

Disney is arguably the reason that the World Cup has increased in popularity, since it heavily promoted the tournament across ABC and ESPN in 2010 and 2014. Controversially, Fox executives were later accused of bribing FIFA in order to secure the 2018 and 2022 games despite offering a lower bid than Disney.

The 2030 tournament will be the 24th FIFA World Cup. It is due to be held from June 8, 2030, to July 21, and will be hosted by Morocco, Portugal, and Spain.

items.title: How to play 'Grand Theft Auto VI' on your iPhone, iPad, or Apple Vision Pro
items.content_html:
In case you didn't know, there are amazing cloud and console streaming options for your Apple products that can easily bring games like "Grand Theft Auto VI" to your iPhone.

There are times when you might want to dive back into Vice City while your TV is occupied, or perhaps while you're away from home. It's possible via game streaming, but there are limitations and considerations to make.

First off, you need to know what streaming platform works with your devices. I like using the app Asobi on iPhone, iPad, and Apple Vision Pro, but there are other options.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

PlayStation has its own Remote Play app that isn't optimized for iPhone Duo, but works great otherwise. You'll want a good local network connection and a physical controller — touch controls just aren't going to cut it.

If you're an Xbox user, the options are a bit more limited. Xbox cloud streaming is limited to the Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, and Xbox One, so you can't stream Grand Theft Auto VI to your iPhone using that platform.

Run Ethernet directly to your console if possible, and for extra-low latency, assign specific ports for your streaming connection. That's a power user move, so if you don't know what that means, don't worry about it.

Local streaming will always work better than cloud streaming, so keep that in mind. Some streaming tools will let you remote stream from different networks, but those connections aren't always reliable.

The PlayStation app isn't optimized for iPhone Duo

AppleInsider highly recommends controllers like Backbone One when using iPhone, or a DualSense 5 or Xbox Core controller for iPad and Apple Vision Pro. iPhone Duo doesn't have a bespoke grip controller for it yet, but propping it up with a DualSense works well too.

Grand Theft Auto VI is an epic experience built to be enjoyed on the biggest TVs with the most dynamic sound systems. That doesn't mean you can't have a good experience on an iPhone with AirPods playing Spatial Audio either.

Sometimes playing a game on the small screen is the only option, but at least it's an option

Streaming with some apps like Asobi in Apple Vision Pro transforms the experience. You can add AI-generated stereoscopic 3D to games, though it's not always a perfect implementation.

However you choose to play, GTA VI is set to be one of the biggest games ever made. Though, while it's possible to play across all of your devices through streaming, don't forget to take a break every now and again too.

items.title: Apple HomeView doesn't need to be portable, but it can be with a battery
items.content_html:
Apple didn't make some weird, proprietary connector or power system for Apple HomeView, but instead relied on USB-C. That little connector opens up a lot of possibility, including battery packs.

A lot of the early rumors around Apple HomeView made it sound like a portable display. At one point it was even suggested that they would be carried around by multiple users in a home instead of being bolted in place.

The product Apple announced was the opposite in nearly every aspect. It is pitched as a stationary speaker like HomePod, but with a display, or a controller that would replace a light switch or smart display.

At first, I wondered if that decision was a bad one, and Apple HomeView should be portable. While it can absolutely work via battery power, I have backed off of that original assumption of it needing to be totally portable.

Here's the thing, Apple HomeView isn't an iPad, and Apple knows that. Making the device portable would break into the confined and deliberate user space Apple has created for the product.

That said, there's still space for a battery in this little display.

The need for a battery base

After spending a week with Apple HomeView, I can easily say it's a stationary device. That constraint forces you to interact with it in the way Apple intended, which I appreciate.

A tiny battery can easily power the Apple HomeView

However, there is at least one place in my home where a portable HomeView would make more sense — the kitchen.

Currently the Apple HomeView is stationed on the counter space situated behind the sink. It's a corner section with a raised shelf, so the display is easily visible from anywhere in the room.

It is a small display though, which limits its utility beyond being a nice photo or album art viewer at a certain distance. I do like that Apple considered the UI so it was easy to view from a distance.

Speaking of, that's another thing the rumors got wrong. The UI was said to adjust based on the user's distance, which was never announced and didn't ship.

Apple HomeView is actually quite static when you're not interacting with it

Anyway, while testing HomeView with a battery pack, I realized having the ability to carry the display from behind the sink to the kitchen island is a nice option. This is where a simple battery base would be amazing.

I've seen some projects made in the 3D printer community that houses a shelf for a standard battery pack, but these are bulky. I'm assuming it is only a matter of time before we see a bespoke battery base made by some third party.

Apple HomeView doesn't need much to power it. The speaker base model needs 30W while the wall-mounted option needs 20W.

My little MagSafe battery for iPhone that has a power cable was able to run the HomeView without issue. Having such a tiny battery for moving HomeView while cooking is more than enough.

A more simple solution

Apple HomeView is such a computationally simple platform that it starts up almost immediately when connected to power. Even if a battery pack is too bulky or ugly, the alternative is more simple.

Remove the USB-C cable and move HomeView to where it's needed

I can see either my wife or I take the HomeView from the sink by unplugging the USB-C cable in the back then moving it to the island. There, attach a USB-C connected to an outlet or battery.

It takes about 15 seconds for it to fully boot and work normally. Sure, losing power for those moments is inconvenient, but it doesn't make the device unusable.

Outside of that use case, I'm not sure what utility having a portable HomeView would provide. We already have iPhones, iPads, Apple Watches, and Macs that can move around with us.

HomePod mini has a few battery base options, so expect HomeView to get some too

By making the Apple HomeView a device that must be connected to power, it creates constraints and limitations. It isn't a tablet you carry around your home, yet another device to charge, or App Store to populate.

Instead, Apple HomeView is a secondary device experience with AirPlay, decent speakers, and an interface that relies on donated apps and widgets. If it were more than that, it would be a different product and potentially confusing.

I plan to try out various battery packs, cases, and other products with Apple HomeView in the future. However, I truly think Apple might have nailed the size and OS constraints in the first iteration to ensure it is the product it says it is.

Sometimes constraints are a good thing.

items.title: Engwe M20 3.0 review: Cruising in style without any smarts
items.content_html:
The Engwe M20 3.0 is a fast, long-range moped-style e-bike that looks great, handles well, and doesn't need to connect to your smartphone. That's either a good or bad thing depending on your needs.

I've been testing e-bikes for AppleInsider for years now, and my latest review unit feels a little out of place in a world of tech-driven products. While you can technically pair Engwe's e-bike with an app, it's a worthless app that requires too much effort to use.

So, I've been using the Engwe without an app, which might be my favorite thing about this e-bike. It works totally fine completely disconnected from a third-party app trying to suck in my location data and show me posts from an in-app social media client.

Sometimes you just need to unplug and ride a bike, even if it's powered by a battery.

That's a big departure from my previous e-bike review, the Velotric GoMad. That one felt custom-made for Apple fans thanks to its Find My and Apple Health integrations.

Engwe's M20 3.0, however, is more tailored to the e-bike enthusiast than the tech one.

Engwe M20 3.0 review: Design

I really like how different the Engwe M20 3.0 looks and feels. It's really more motorcycle than moped, but the pedals give it away.


Engwe M20 3.0 review: A well-designed bike that turns heads

The dual headlights on the front are big and bright. They automatically turn on using a light sensor, though they can be toggled as well.

This is my first e-bike with a long seat that can hold two people. Though, given I'm 6 foot tall at 230 pounds, my passenger would need to weigh less than 100 pounds to meet the 330 pound weight capacity.

There are rear pegs for that potential passenger though.

The seat is only 31 inches high, but you do have to swing your leg wide to mount the bike given the length. The 41-inch height of the handlebars are perfect for comfortable cruising or leaning in for some speed.


Engwe M20 3.0 review: A long seat for comfy riding

This is an incredibly heavy bike though at 102 pounds, which appears to be the weight with both batteries installed. That weight is felt more when moving the bike around than when riding.

The Engwe M20 3.0 comes equipped with 20-inch by 4-inch puncture-resistant fat tires. I tend to like bigger tires, but these work great on this body style.

There's also a little tank bag that I've opened once and never opened again. I'm not a fan of carrying keys, but I'm sure this little addition will be useful for some.

Engwe M20 3.0 review: Features

The Engwe M20 3.0 packs a 3,300W peak output motor with 120Nm of torque. It can house two 60V 20Ah batteries for up to 180 miles on a single charge.


Engwe M20 3.0 review: A powerful motor and dual batteries for long range

You can go up to 40 MPH on this e-bike, but I'm quite content hitting about 28 MPH in most situations. It takes off fast too, hitting 15 MPH in just a couple of seconds.

The 3.5-inch display is bright and easy to read. I don't ride with my iPhone on the handlebars anymore, but I don't miss it thanks to my Apple Watch.

You can control all of the bike's settings from the display by holding the "M" button to get to the menu. There's not much to control beyond customizing some of the speed limits.

I'm happy with the default settings and never going over 30 MPH. The higher speeds feel too dangerous, even on paved roads, and the higher speeds use the battery faster anyway.


Engwe M20 3.0 review: A bright and easily-read display

While this is a fast and powerful bike, the brake system is equally impressive. It has a four-piston braking system that can let you stop nearly on a dime.

There is also full suspension, which I always appreciate in my e-bikes.

Charge one battery to 80% in 2 hours or both batteries to 80% in four hours. The charger is one of those with a loud fan, but it isn't a problem since you'll be charging it somewhere like a garage anyway.

Riding Engwe M20 3.0

I'll reiterate it here just in case you missed it, but Engwe does offer an app. I opened it, saw I had to provide order details and a serial number to pair it, then immediately closed and deleted it.


Engwe M20 3.0 review: Big but not too bulky for parking in tight spots

The app seems to have GPS tracking and one of those dumb in-app social networks. Both are things I never use, and I recommend you don't either.

Anyway, the Engwe M20 3.0 works great without an app. I'm glad that e-bikes haven't been ruined by required apps, but I'm sure that's coming at some point.

You can set a password that shows up at startup too, which is a nice little extra protection.


Engwe M20 3.0 review: No need for an app when there are simple controls

The bike itself is comfortable to sit on and ride. Because of its seat, it might be one of the most comfortable e-bikes I've ridden. The suspension helps of course.

Engwe's website shows people riding this thing like a dirt bike on trails and ramps, but I'm never going to do that and I doubt most people would. It's probably possible, but really this is great as a city cruiser.

I'm glad that the Engwe can easily hit speeds over 25 MPH. It makes me feel much more confident on the road when I'm sharing it with vehicles.


Engwe M20 3.0 review: Bright headlights makes riding at night feel safer

Most places I'm riding don't have speed limits over 30 MPH, so I'm happy to be able to mostly keep up with traffic. Of course, there's always that one person upset they can't recklessly go double the speed limit.

The fat tires, wide-set handlebars, bright headlights, and long range all make me feel confident when I ride. It's also nice that the design feels unique compared to some other e-bikes I've tested that all feel a little same-y.

As always, I'll happily point out that there are turn signals and brake lights. These feel like a must on any modern e-bike and I'll automatically knock off points if they're not there.

Ditching smarts for a better ride

While there are smart features available, the app feels so generic and access is annoyingly frustrating I'm happy to have avoided it for this e-bike. I can attach sensors to a pedal and rear wheel for improved workout metrics, plus I can hide an AirTag somewhere too.


Engwe M20 3.0 review: An e-bike for bike enthusiasts

No app means no weird privacy concerns over data collection either. I also would prefer just never be bombarded by a bike app again to look at a sale or some random person's post about a ride they completed today.

The Engwe M20 3.0 has been a refreshing product in a world that demands we interact with some kind of tech or app at every turn. It's an e-bike that focuses on being a good bike rather than being a good piece of tech.

I'm sure there are plenty of you out there that will appreciate that as much as I have.

Engwe M20 3.0 review - Pros

  • Incredible range and speed
  • Fat tires, suspension, and a long seat make for a comfy ride
  • Can rely heavily on the throttle since there's so much battery capacity
  • Fast launching and high speeds make it feel safer to ride along with traffic

Engwe M20 3.0 review - Cons

  • An app experience so terrible I ignored it
  • This is a very heavy e-bike — beware

Rating: 4 out of 5

This is a tech website so I'll acknowledge it's funny to praise an e-bike with an app so worthless I ignored it. Though, the design and specs of this particular e-bike more than make up for that and make riding fun.

Where to buy the Engwe M20 3.0

Get the Engwe M20 3.0 e-bike from Engwe's website for a discounted $1,529.10 with dual batteries or $1,259.10 with a single battery when you use promo code APPLEINSIDER at checkout.

It is also available on Amazon in the same configurations: $1,699 for dual batteries or $1,399 for a single battery.

items.title: Apple AI agents are coming to help you code, browse, & perform tasks
items.content_html:
A new report based on a job listing shares what everyone already expected — that Apple will soon be joining other AI companies in offering agentic solutions to everyday tasks including coding.

Apple is already building out a system for Siri and Apple Intelligence to control every aspect of your device through app intents. The clear next step after that is providing an AI tool that will perform tasks without user input.

According to a report from Bloomberg based on a new Apple job listing, Apple is seeking out an engineer manager to develop an agentic AI assistant. There's nothing else to this story other than Apple literally seeking such a person out and every other AI company offering similar products.

It isn't clear when Apple might offer an agentic AI model, but guesses put such a launch sometime in 2027. It's likely a key feature of the OS 28 cycle.

"Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does," the job listing reportedly reads. "It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple."

It's a detailed listing that outlines already-known Apple parameters for AI, including privacy and security. The company is very concerned with how users are letting third-party AI bots control their machines and has been developing tools to give users more control over potentially rogue AI agents.

The feature could always be revealed sooner, as it seems Apple is much more ready to debut features when they are ready under CEO John Ternus. Time will tell.

items.title: 'Wild Things' to tell the story of Siegfried & Roy on Apple TV in April 2027
items.content_html:
Andrew Garfield and Jude Law play the iconic illusionist duo Siegfried and Roy in a new Apple TV series coming in April 2027.

On Thursday, after revealing that F1 Academy races would stream on Apple TV through 2027, Apple announced a new show is coming to its streaming platform. "Wild Things," created and directed by John Hoffman, tells the story of magicians Siegfried and Roy.

Jude Law plays Siegfried, while Garfield stars as Roy. Apple has released a teaser trailer for "Wild Things," and the company says the show will premiere on Apple TV on Friday, April 16, 2027.

Inspired by the wild true story. Jude Law and Andrew Garfield are Siegfried & Roy.

#WildThings premieres April 16 on Apple TV.

— Apple TV (@AppleTV) November 19, 2026

Law and Garfield, in their roles as Siegfried and Roy, "push the concept of illusion versus reality to the extreme, both personally and professionally," says Apple, "until tragedy reframes their story and opens a mystery surrounding their last fateful Las Vegas show."

John Hoffman, known for "Only Murders in the Building" and "Looking," is the writer, showrunner, and executive producer for "Wild Things." Other executive producers include Brian Grazer, Tony Leonidis, Kathy Ciric, Will Malnati, and Steven Leckart, alongside cast members Jude Law and Andrew Garfield.

"Wild Things" takes inspiration from a 2022 eight-episode podcast, similarly dubbed "Wild Things: Siegfried and Roy." The podcast is already available on the Apple Podcasts app for those looking to learn all about the lives of Siegfried and Roy.

While the show "Wild Things" won't be available until April 2027, Apple's streaming service offers an extensive library of other shows and films. Some of them, like "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving," are occasionally made available for free.

items.title: How to keep watching DVDs with VLC as Apple phases out Mac DVD support
items.content_html:
Apple has started retiring the technology behind its built-in DVD playback starting in macOS 27. Here's how you can still watch discs on a Mac with an optical drive and VLC.

For now, the change affects developers, not people watching DVDs on their Macs. Apple has removed the DVDPlayback framework from the macOS 27 SDK, so developers can no longer build apps against it with that SDK.

The framework itself remains in macOS 27, and Apple says it won't be removed until a future release. DVD Player also remains available and functional in macOS 27.

If you have movies on DVD, you don't have to wait for another macOS update to find a different way to play them. The free VLC app can open a DVD as a disc, giving you access to its movie, menus, chapters, audio tracks, and subtitles.

You'll need an external optical drive that can read DVDs.

Get the right drive and disc

Before downloading anything, check the optical drive you plan to use. A drive that reads DVDs will usually read CDs too, but a CD-only drive can't read a DVD.

If you're using a drive you already own, check its model information or specifications to see which discs it supports. Check the connector too, because a USB-A drive needs an adapter or hub if your Mac only has USB-C ports.

If the drive includes a second power cable or its own power supply, use it according to the manufacturer's instructions. Optical drives can be sensitive to power and connection problems.

If the drive repeatedly disconnects, fails to spin up, or disappears after you insert a DVD, connect the drive directly to the Mac instead of through a hub. A direct connection can rule out a power or connection problem before you start changing VLC settings.

Apple has separate connection instructions for its USB SuperDrive, including the adapters it supports with USB-C Macs. If you use another manufacturer's drive, check its instructions because the power and adapter requirements may be different.

Check the disc too, because a DVD movie usually uses the DVD-Video format to organize its menu, feature, chapters, and extras. In VLC, open a DVD-Video disc with File, Open Disc.

For a data DVD, open the individual video file you want to watch, since VLC handles those differently from DVD-Video discs. You'll also want to confirm that you're working with a DVD and not a Blu-ray disc.

A DVD-only drive can't read Blu-ray, even though the discs are about the same size. A Blu-ray-capable drive solves that hardware problem, but commercial Blu-ray playback has its own requirements and isn't covered by the DVD steps below.

Install VLC on your Mac

Download VLC from VideoLAN's official Mac page. There are downloads for Intel and Apple Silicon Macs, plus a universal version that works on either.

The universal download is an easy choice if you aren't sure which processor your Mac has.

  1. Download VLC for macOS from VideoLAN.
  2. Open the downloaded .dmg file.
  3. Drag the VLC app into the Applications folder shown in the installer window.
  4. Open VLC from Applications. If macOS verifies the app on its first launch, let it finish and choose Open when prompted.

Keep VLC in Applications once you've installed it. That way, the app will still be there after you eject the installer disk image or clear out your Downloads folder.

Installing VLC doesn't remove Apple's DVD Player or make VLC the automatic choice when you insert a DVD. You can leave your Mac's settings alone and open a disc in VLC whenever you want.

You also don't need to install a separate codec pack before trying VLC.

Play a DVD in VLC

Connect the optical drive and insert your movie DVD, and give the Mac a moment to read it. If DVD Player opens automatically, close its movie window or quit the app before opening the same disc in VLC.

  1. Open VLC.
  2. Choose File & Open Disc from the menu bar.
  3. Choose DVD as the disc type.
  4. Check that VLC has selected the drive containing your movie, particularly if you have more than one optical drive connected.
  5. Open the selected disc to start playback.

Don't worry if the feature doesn't begin immediately. The DVD might show a studio logo, trailers, a warning screen, or its main menu first. When the menu appears, choose its on-screen Play option, just as you would with a DVD player connected to a television.

The Open Disc step lets VLC treat the DVD as a movie rather than a collection of files. A DVD's navigation tells the player how its feature, chapters, extras, and menu fit together. Double-clicking one video file inside the disc might play a clip, but it can leave you without the movie's normal controls.

After swapping DVDs, stop the first movie and open the new disc. VLC may still be pointed at the earlier selection if you leave it running while changing discs. Check the selected drive again if you've connected more than one.

Find the movie and move between chapters

A DVD's own menu is usually the easiest place to find its main feature, scene selection, and bonus material. Each disc arranges those choices differently. Some start the movie on their own, while others wait for you to choose Play.

VLC also lets you move through a disc from its Playback menu. DVD content is divided into titles, which can be separate movies, episodes, or extras, while each title can contain chapters for individual scenes.

If VLC opens the wrong thing, try another title until you find the feature. Titles may appear only as numbers, and some discs list previews or other short videos before the main movie.

If you've found the feature but want to skip to a particular scene, move between its chapters or use the DVD's scene-selection menu. When you can't tell which title you want, return to the DVD's on-screen menu and choose the movie there.

Use VLC's playback controls to pause, resume, or change the volume. Once the movie starts, you can switch to full-screen viewing. When you're finished, stop playback before ejecting the disc.

If macOS says the disc is still in use, close the movie in VLC or quit the app and try again.

Change the audio or subtitles

Some DVDs carry several audio tracks. VLC's Audio menu lets you choose among the tracks available on the disc, which could include another language, a commentary, or a different sound mix.

A commentary track can catch you off guard if it's selected when the movie starts. If you hear people discussing the film over its dialogue, switch audio tracks before troubleshooting your speakers. If there's no sound at all, check VLC's volume and your Mac's selected sound output too.

For subtitles, open VLC's Subtitle menu and choose a track or turn subtitles off. VLC can show the tracks supplied on the DVD, but it can't add a language the disc doesn't contain.

Some DVDs also put subtitle and language choices in their own on-screen setup menus. DVD subtitles are often stored as images instead of ordinary text.

Because of that, VLC font settings for separate subtitle files may not affect subtitles built into the DVD. You can try another subtitle track if the disc includes one, but you generally can't change the font embedded in the DVD itself.

Make VLC your choice when you insert a DVD

You don't have to change a Mac setting to use VLC. If Apple's DVD Player opens when you insert a movie, quit it and choose File, Open Disc in VLC. That's enough if you watch DVDs only occasionally.

For regular use, connect the optical drive and open System Settings, CDs & DVDs. Find the action for inserting a video DVD, then choose the available option that fits how you want to open discs.

You can select another app where macOS offers that choice, or have the Mac wait for you to open the disc yourself. If you can't find CDs & DVDs in System Settings, check that the optical drive is connected.

Apple says the DVD-related settings section won't appear unless a drive is connected, so check again after your Mac recognizes it. The setting is separate from choosing VLC as the default app for individual video files.

Changing a file's default app affects what happens when you open files of that type. The disc-insertion setting controls what your Mac does when you put a DVD into an optical drive.

What to do when the Mac can't find your DVD

Start with the drive and make sure it's connected, has enough power, and responds when you insert a disc. If it never spins up, keeps disconnecting, or can't read any disc, VLC won't have anything to play.

Try a second DVD that you know works to see where the problem is. If neither disc reads, the issue is likely with the cable, adapter, hub, or drive, while a working second DVD points to dirt or damage on the first disc.

Home-recorded discs can introduce another variable. Drives differ in which recordable DVD formats they support, so a drive that plays a commercial movie may still struggle with a particular burned disc.

If Finder shows the DVD but VLC doesn't find it, reopen File & Open Disc and make sure VLC has selected the correct drive. Finder only confirms that macOS recognizes a disc, which doesn't guarantee VLC is pointing to the right drive after you swap discs.

What to do when the DVD opens but won't play

First, determine whether you're opening a DVD movie or a data disc. If Finder shows individual video files, open the file you want directly in VLC.

However, if the disc contains a VIDEO_TS folder, open it as a DVD so VLC can use the disc's movie navigation.

A DVD that reaches its menu presents a different problem from one the Mac can't read. Try the menu's on-screen Play option. If VLC starts an extra or trailer instead of the feature, look at the available titles or return to the disc menu to select the main movie.

Region codes can also block DVDs bought in another country. Some drives enforce the selected region before VLC can read the disc, and Apple says you can change a DVD drive's region only five times before the final choice becomes permanent, so read any region-change prompt carefully.

If several other movie DVDs work and only one fails, focus on that disc. Damage, dirt, or unusual DVD authoring can prevent the movie from loading or interrupt only part of it.

Check whether the failure follows the disc before changing settings that affect every movie you play.

What macOS 27 changes for DVD playback

Apple's macOS 27 release notes say developers can no longer build against the DVDPlayback framework with the macOS 27 SDK. Apple also says the framework itself will be removed from macOS in a future release.

DVD Player still works in macOS 27. Apple hasn't announced an end date for the app, and macOS 27 can still recognize DVDs through a compatible optical drive.

VLC gives you another way to handle playback without depending on Apple's long-term plans for DVD Player. Once the Mac can read the disc, VLC can open the DVD and give you access to its movie, menus, chapters, audio tracks, and subtitles.
